references.text: Jesus says that whoever has left everything for the sake of God's kingdom will receive 'a hundredfold' in this time and 'eternal life' in the age to come. The parallel passages in the other Gospels expand on this promise: [ref:Matt 19:29|Matthew 19:29] and [ref:Mark 10:30|Mark 10:30].

Matthew's parallel to Luke 18:30: 'Everyone who has left house or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or fields for my name's sake will receive a hundredfold and inherit eternal life.' The same promise of abundant reward and eternal life.

Mark's parallel passage expands the promise with an explicit distinction between reward 'now in this time' and 'eternal life in the age to come,' which corresponds exactly to Luke's wording about 'this time' and 'the coming age.'

The expert in the law asks Jesus: 'What must I do to inherit eternal life?' (ζωὴν αἰώνιον). The same expression as in [ref:Luk 18:30|Luke 18:30], where eternal life is promised to those who follow Jesus.

The context of the promise: the rich man asks Jesus, 'What must I do to inherit eternal life?' – the same eternal life that Jesus promises in verse 30 to those who leave everything for the sake of God's kingdom.

Jesus says: 'I give them eternal life; they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.' Eternal life as Jesus' gift to those who follow him, just as promised in [ref:Luk 18:30|Luke 18:30].

Paul writes that 'the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.' The same contrast between 'this time' (ἐν τῷ καιρῷ τούτῳ) and the coming glory as in Luke 18:30.

'For our light and momentary troubles are achieving for us an eternal glory that far outweighs them all.' The idea that present sacrifices lead to eternal reward corresponds to Jesus' promise in [ref:Luk 18:30|Luke 18:30].
Paul speaks of a promise for both 'the life that now is and for the one to come' – a parallel to Jesus' distinction between reward in this time and in the age to come.

Daniel prophesies about the resurrection: 'Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.' Eternal life (חַיֵּי עוֹלָם) as an eschatological promise – the background for Jesus' use of the expression ζωὴν αἰώνιον in [ref:Luk 18:30|Luke 18:30].

The Letter to the Hebrews speaks of having 'tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come' – 'the coming age' (τῷ αἰῶνι τῷ ἐρχομένῳ) that Jesus refers to in [ref:Luk 18:30|Luke 18:30].
